rows.item: Opening quotation (Pérez-González, 2014): audiovisual texts shape almost everyone’s life; audiences look for aesthetic and emotional experiences; viewing has become more varied
rows.note: The long quotation became one short sentence with the source kept; the points on emotions, memories and variety were left out for simplicity.

rows.item: Audiovisual translation as the fastest-growing strand of Translation Studies in the last fifteen years
rows.note: Softened to “one of the fastest-growing areas”, and the fifteen-year span was removed because it goes out of date.

rows.item: Four signs of growth: more research literature, undergraduate modules, postgraduate courses and PhDs, conferences
rows.note: Academic background that beginners do not need.

rows.item: What prompted the growth: the development of communication technology, more exposure to visual semiotics, and the link between AVT and technological innovation
rows.note: Shortened to the role of technology (“Driven by technology”, “It depends heavily on technology”).

rows.item: The needs created by technology: theoretical frameworks, new research methods for audiovisual data, understanding new discourse communities
rows.note: Research-level content that beginners do not need.

rows.item: What is so special about AVT: three relationships (words with pictures and soundtrack; foreign with target language and culture; spoken with written code) (Gambier, 2003)
rows.note: Only the link between words, pictures and sound is kept, with Gambier (2003); the spoken-to-written point is in Chapter 27, and the foreign-to-target culture point is not used.

rows.item: Earlier names: film translation (before television and video), language transfer (ignored images, music and sound effects), screen translation (“too narrow”, O’Hagan 2007), multimedia translation (games, theatre, comics, CD-ROMs)
rows.note: The history of the names is not needed at beginner level; the handbook uses only “audiovisual translation”.

rows.item: Audiovisual translation (AVT) as the most widely used term
rows.where: Chapter 26, Step 1; Words to remember, Chapter 26; Abbreviations
rows.note: Kept as the name used throughout, with a simple definition and the Arabic {{الترجمة السمعية البصرية}} added.

rows.item: “AVT, translation or adaptation?”: why some scholars see AVT as adaptation because of spatial and temporal limits
rows.note: The debate is for advanced readers; the practical limits of space and time appear in Chapter 26, Step 4 and Chapter 27, Step 1.

rows.item: Subtitles change the mode from oral to written and often omit words of the original
rows.note: Turned into practical advice: condense the speech (Step 2) and cut it down to short written lines (Step 3).

rows.item: Dubbing ({{الدبلجة}}): replaces the source dialogue track with a target-language track; lip-synchronisation when the face or chest is visible in a medium shot
rows.where: Chapter 26, Step 2; Words to remember, Chapter 26
rows.note: Shortened to new dialogue “often matched to the actors’ lips”; the medium-shot detail was left out.

rows.item: Voice-over (half dubbing), with the Arabic gloss {{المعلق}} (for example, matches): documentaries, interviews and programmes translated and broadcast almost in time with the original, the original voice reduced
rows.where: Chapter 26, Step 2; Words to remember, Chapter 26
rows.note: Kept with the documentary example; the Arabic term became {{التعليق الصوتي}} and “half dubbing” was dropped.

rows.item: Free commentary: an adaptation for a new audience with additions, clarifications, omissions and comments; used for children’s programmes, documentaries and promotional videos
rows.note: The handbook introduces only four main types for beginners.

rows.item: In-vision signing, for the deaf and hard of hearing
rows.note: Not one of the four main types the handbook introduces; subtitles for the deaf and hard of hearing (SDH) are mentioned in Chapter 27.

rows.item: Audio description, for the blind and partially sighted: describing action, body language, facial expressions and costumes
rows.where: Chapter 26, Step 2; Words to remember, Chapter 26
rows.note: Shortened to “a spoken description of the action”, and the Arabic {{الوصف الصوتي}} was added; it is also a Try it question.

rows.item: Audio-subtitling: subtitles spoken by an actor or a speech synthesiser
rows.note: Not one of the four main types the handbook introduces.

rows.item: Four YouTube links as examples
rows.note: The links were not checked; the handbook gives its own examples instead.

rows.item: 1. Introduction: AVT is in high demand because of the development of communication and translation and its link with technological innovation; AVT and technology go hand in hand
rows.note: Shortened to one idea: AVT is driven by technology and depends on it.

rows.item: 1. Early days: researchers were interested in filmmakers; today they are interested in pleasing the audience
rows.note: Research history that beginners do not need.

rows.item: 1. Why AVT is special: the only type of translation that relies entirely on technology
rows.note: Softened to “It depends heavily on technology”, because “the only” and “entirely” are too absolute.

rows.item: 1. Why AVT is special: the only type with more than one element (visual, audio, textual), all working together to create meaning
rows.where: Chapter 26, Step 1 (second bullet); Try it and Remember, Chapter 26
rows.note: Kept as images, sound and written words working together; the claim that it is the “only” type was dropped.

rows.item: 1. Why AVT is special: it links a foreign language and culture (possibly informal) with a target language and culture (possibly formal)
rows.note: Not needed at beginner level; the differences between the two languages are covered in Chapter 4 and Chapter 26, Step 4.

rows.item: 1. Why AVT is special: the only type in which the medium may change, such as from spoken to written language
rows.note: Kept as “Speech must be cut down to short written lines”, applied to subtitles; “only” was dropped.

rows.item: 2.1 Film translation: the term used before television spread
rows.note: The history of the names is not needed; the handbook uses only “audiovisual translation”.

rows.item: 2.2 Language transfer: focused on language and ignored images, music and sound effects
rows.note: The history of the names is not needed at beginner level.

rows.item: 2.3 Screen translation: later a widely used term
rows.note: The history of the names is not needed at beginner level.

rows.item: 2.4 Multimedia translation: includes games, theatre, comics and digital resources
rows.note: The history of the names is not needed at beginner level.

rows.item: 2.5 Audiovisual translation: now the most common term
rows.where: Chapter 26, Step 1; Words to remember, Chapter 26
rows.note: Kept as the term used throughout, with a definition and the Arabic {{الترجمة السمعية البصرية}} added.

rows.item: 3.1 Subtitling: a change of mode from oral to written language, often omitting words of the original
rows.where: Chapter 26, Step 2; Chapter 27 (Words to remember, Steps 2 and 3)
rows.note: Shown as one of four main types with a chapter of its own; the definition also covers on-screen text and song lyrics, and the Arabic {{السترجة}} / {{الترجمة المرئية}} was added.

rows.item: 3.2 Dubbing: replaces source-language dialogue with target-language dialogue
rows.where: Chapter 26, Step 2; Words to remember, Chapter 26
rows.note: Kept, with lip-matching mentioned and the Arabic {{الدبلجة}} added.

rows.item: 3.3 Voice-over: also called half dubbing, common in documentaries; the original voice is reduced or lowered; voice actors generally not used
rows.where: Chapter 26, Step 2; Words to remember, Chapter 26
rows.note: The documentary example is kept; “half dubbing” and the remark on voice actors were left out, and the Arabic {{التعليق الصوتي}} was added.

rows.item: 3.4 Free commentary: adapts content for a new audience and may add to it; football commentary as an example
rows.note: The handbook introduces only four main types for beginners.

rows.item: 3.5 In-vision signing: for deaf and hard-of-hearing audiences
rows.note: The handbook introduces only four main types for beginners.

rows.item: 3.6 Audio description: for blind and partially sighted audiences; the translator describes the characters’ actions and visual events
rows.where: Chapter 26, Step 2; Words to remember and Try it, Chapter 26
rows.note: Kept in one line, with the Arabic {{الوصف الصوتي}} added.

rows.item: 3.7 Audio subtitling: reading subtitles aloud for blind and partially sighted audiences
rows.note: The handbook introduces only four main types for beginners.

rows.item: 4.1 Skopos Theory: skopos means “aim” or “goal”; developed by Hans J. Vermeer; the aim is to fulfil the purpose set by the client, even by changing parts of the translation
rows.where: Chapter 26, Step 3; Words to remember, Chapter 26
rows.note: Kept as “the purpose of a translation decides how it is translated”, credited to Reiss and Vermeer (1984), with the Arabic {{نظرية الغاية}}; the meaning of the word skopos and the changing of parts were left out.

rows.item: 4.1 Skopos Theory: emphasis on function (“How will the translation function for the target audience?”); the key elements are the client and the target audience
rows.note: Turned into practical questions (what is it for, who will watch it, ask for the brief); the client’s role is taught in Chapter 2.

rows.item: 4.1 Skopos Theory aligns with dynamic equivalence, which seeks to give the audience the same emotions
rows.note: Not needed at beginner level; the chapter keeps one simple idea.

rows.item: 4.2 Descriptive Translation Studies (DTS): describes existing translations and why translators chose as they did; key aspects (for example humour subtitled from English into Arabic, norms, comparing source and target, quality assessment)
rows.note: Advanced theory; the AVT chapters keep only Skopos theory.

rows.item: 4.3 Reception Studies: the audience’s reception and interpretation of translated audiovisual content; key aspects (viewer preferences, surveys, feedback loops, accessibility)
rows.note: Advanced theory; the AVT chapters keep only Skopos theory.

rows.item: 4.4 Polysystem Theory (Multi-System Theory, Even-Zohar): how cultural and literary systems influence one another; key aspects (norms, conflict, cultural transfer)
rows.note: Advanced theory; the AVT chapters keep only Skopos theory.

rows.item: 5. Challenges: AVT needs linguistic, cultural, technical and creative skills at the same time
rows.note: Became a step with four short bullets: culture, language, technology, creativity.

rows.item: 5.1 Cultural differences: bridging the gap between cultures; references with no direct equivalent
rows.note: Shortened to one line, with links to Chapters 15 to 17.

rows.item: 5.2 Linguistic differences: different grammar and vocabulary; complex dialogue must stay accurate, natural and concise
rows.note: Shortened to “accurate and brief”, with a link to Chapter 4.

rows.item: 5.3 Technical constraints: subtitles and captions are limited by space and time
rows.note: Kept in one line; the actual limits are explained in Chapter 27.

rows.item: 5.4 Creative demands: translators must often be creative
rows.note: Kept and joined with the list of hard items (jokes, wordplay, songs, slang).

rows.item: 5.5 Translating from English into Arabic: linguistic, cultural and technical differences
rows.note: Merged into the four general challenges instead of a separate English-to-Arabic heading.

rows.item: 5.5 Hard items: jokes, humour, wordplay, irony, sarcasm, songs, religious texts, slang, political speeches
rows.note: Only jokes, wordplay, songs and slang were kept; humour, irony, sarcasm, religious texts and political speeches were left out for space.

rows.item: 6.1 Introduction and main idea: digital screens have replaced paper; the Arab world needs to adopt AVT more fully, update translation policies and train specialists
rows.note: A policy discussion beyond a beginner’s handbook, and the notes name no source for it.

rows.item: 6.2 The Arab context: a large young population and high illiteracy, so print translation is not enough; AVT as infotainment, largely overlooked by institutions
rows.note: A policy discussion beyond a beginner’s handbook, and the notes name no source for it.

rows.item: 6.3 Challenges to localising AVT: lack of definition and institutional reluctance; policy and vision deficits; linguistic and cultural context; technological shifts; the risk that AVT studies look imported
rows.note: A policy discussion beyond a beginner’s handbook, and the notes name no source for it.

rows.item: 6.4 Missed opportunities: film and international recognition (poor subtitling and awards), online presence, accessibility for disabled audiences, tourism, regional contrasts
rows.note: A policy discussion beyond a beginner’s handbook, and the notes name no source for it.

rows.item: 6.5 Research and education deficits: research that is too theoretical; neglected software skills, job-market needs and translation from Arabic; the gap between academia and industry; live news subtitling and pilgrimage translation services
rows.note: Advice for universities rather than for beginner translators, and the notes name no source for it.

rows.item: 6.6 Educational solutions: teach creative translation (for example film titles); host AVT conferences, update curricula, link academia and industry, share Arab culture through digital media
rows.note: Advice for universities rather than for beginner translators, and the notes name no source for it.

rows.item: 7. Introduction to dubbing: one of the oldest modes of AVT, widely used in Europe, America and Asia
rows.note: Not kept; the handbook’s sentence on dubbing gives an Arab-world example instead.

rows.item: 7. Dubbing replaces the original soundtrack of source-language dialogue with a new soundtrack of target-language dialogue
rows.where: Words to remember, Chapter 26; Chapter 26, Step 2
rows.note: Kept in one short definition.

rows.item: 7. Dubbing is commonly used in cartoons, video games and commercials
rows.note: “Video games” became “games”, and the sentence was joined to an Arab-world example.

rows.item: 7.1 Types of dubbing and revoicing: dubbing (fully replaced), voice-over (translation heard over the original voice), audio description (scenes described for blind audiences)
rows.note: Only these three are kept, in a simple list together with subtitling.

rows.item: 7.1 Partial dubbing (only the main character is dubbed) and fandubbing (homemade dubbing by fans)
rows.note: Specialised types that beginners do not need.

rows.item: 7.1 Free commentary (extra information beyond the speaker’s words) and audio subtitling (reading subtitles aloud)
rows.note: The handbook introduces only four main types for beginners.

rows.item: 7.1 Interpreting: the live translation of spoken language or sign language
rows.note: Not shown as a type of AVT; interpreting is explained in Chapter 1 as translating speech.

rows.item: 7.2 Challenges in dubbing: language and lip synchronisation; cultural adaptation and context; quality control and consistency
rows.note: Shortened to one sentence: matching lip movements, adapting cultural content and staying consistent across a series.

rows.item: 8. Introduction to subtitling: written text in the lower part of the screen conveying spoken dialogue, images and soundtrack information
rows.where: Words to remember, Chapter 27; Chapter 27, Step 1
rows.note: Rewritten as the dialogue shown at the bottom of the screen with important on-screen text and song lyrics, with the Arabic added.

rows.item: 8. Subtitles generally have 32 to 41 characters per line and at most two lines
rows.note: Corrected to about 37 to 39 characters per line (up to 42 on some platforms), with a reminder to follow the client’s or platform’s style guide; two lines kept.

rows.item: 8.1 Linguistic parameters: intralingual subtitles (same language) and interlingual subtitles (source into target language)
rows.note: Examples added: subtitles for the deaf and hard of hearing (SDH) and for language learners; interlingual described as what translators usually make.

rows.item: 8.1 Linguistic parameters: bilingual subtitles (two languages in one video) and multilingual subtitles (three to seven languages)
rows.note: Specialised kinds that beginners do not need.

rows.item: 8.1 Preparation time: pre-prepared (offline) and live (online) subtitles
rows.note: Same two kinds; only a short example (live news) was added.

rows.item: 8.1 Technical parameters: open (burned-in) subtitles and closed subtitles that can be removed
rows.note: Wording made clearer: closed subtitles “can be turned on and off”.

rows.item: 8.2 Surtitles (live performances) and fansubs (subtitles made by fans)
rows.note: Specialised kinds that beginners do not need.

rows.item: 8.2 Intertitles: printed title cards between scenes in silent films
rows.note: Became a short fact box, with a sentence added on how distributors replaced the cards for foreign showings.

rows.item: 9. The semiotics of subtitling: semiotics is the study of signs
rows.note: Technical term left out; Chapter 27, Step 3 explains in plain words how the images and sound work with the subtitle.

rows.item: 9.1 Visual presentation: verbal signs (with words) and non-verbal signs (without words)
rows.where: Chapter 26, Step 1 (second bullet); Chapter 27, Step 3 (fourth bullet)
rows.note: The terms “verbal” and “non-verbal” were replaced by plain words: images and written words on screen.

rows.item: 9.2 Acoustic presentation: verbal signs (dialogue) and non-verbal signs (sound effects)
rows.where: Chapter 26, Step 1 (second bullet); Chapter 27, Step 3 (fourth bullet)
rows.note: The terms were replaced by plain words: dialogue, music and sound effects.

rows.item: 9.3 Anchoring: verbal information clarifies visual information
rows.note: The term was left out; kept as one tip: the subtitle must still match what is on screen.

rows.item: 9.4 Redundancy: the visual and verbal modes give the same meaning without adding information
rows.note: The term was left out; kept as the tip that a subtitle can be shorter when the picture already shows the meaning.

rows.item: 9.5 Semiotic cohesion: the relationship between dialogue, images and narrative context; subtitles are less coherent without visual support
rows.note: Technical concept that beginners do not need.

rows.item: 9.6 Subtitling vulnerability and change of medium from speech to writing
rows.where: Chapter 27, Step 3 (“It is not easy” paragraph); Try it, Chapter 27
rows.note: Explained in plain words: viewers hear the original and read the translation, so they notice mistakes, and speech must be cut down to short written lines.

rows.item: 9.6 Speech may be scripted or spontaneous (everyday conversation, television news)
rows.note: Detail that beginners do not need.

rows.item: 9.7 Dialogue lists: a written script of everything spoken in a film, used by producers to help translation
rows.where: Words to remember and Step 2, Chapter 27; Chapter 26, Step 5
rows.note: Kept as a key term with the Arabic {{قائمة الحوار}} added and described as a script given to the translator.

rows.item: 10. Linguistic variation: the language of characters shows their personality and background
rows.where: Chapter 27, Step 3 (“It is not easy” paragraph)
rows.note: Kept in one sentence: how characters speak shows who they are.

rows.item: 10.1 Linguistic meaning: denotative (literal) and connotative (emotional and cultural) meaning
rows.note: Not repeated in the AVT chapters; denotation and connotation are taught in Chapter 6.

rows.item: 10.2 Marked speech: taboo words, swear words and emotionally charged utterances
rows.note: The term “marked speech” was left out; swearing and forbidden words are treated under taboo language.

rows.item: 10.3 Sociolect: a variety of language linked to a social group or class
rows.where: Chapter 27, Step 3 (“It is not easy” paragraph)
rows.note: Explained as “social group”, with advice to keep it in the subtitles through word choice.

rows.item: 10.4 Slang: a type of jargon
rows.where: Chapter 27, Step 3 (“It is not easy” paragraph); Chapter 26, Step 4
rows.note: Slang is named as part of how characters speak, but the definition “a type of jargon” was not carried over.

rows.item: 10.5 Idiolect: the speech habits of an individual speaker
rows.where: Chapter 27, Step 3 (“It is not easy” paragraph)
rows.note: Explained as a speaker’s “personal habits”.

rows.item: 11. Culture-bound terms: extralinguistic references linked to a particular culture
rows.where: Words to remember, Chapter 27; Chapter 27, Step 4
rows.note: Defined simply as a reference to something from one culture, with the Arabic {{مصطلح ذو خصوصية ثقافية}} added and a link to Chapter 15.

rows.item: 11.1 Sources of cultural references: geographical; ethnographic (traditional food, holidays); sociopolitical (governmental or social institutions)
rows.note: Cited to Díaz Cintas and Remael (2007), with the examples widened to daily life and government.

rows.item: 12.1 Pedersen’s strategies: retention, specification, direct translation (calque), generalisation, substitution, omission, official equivalent
rows.note: Merged with the second list into eight strategies with both names shown, such as “Loan (retention)” and “Calque (direct translation)”, and cited to Pedersen (2011).

rows.item: 12.2 Díaz Cintas and Remael’s strategies: loan, calque, explicitation, substitution, compensation, omission
rows.note: Six of the nine strategies are kept in the merged list, cited to Díaz Cintas and Remael (2007).

rows.item: 12.2 Díaz Cintas and Remael’s strategies: transposition, lexical recreation, addition
rows.note: Left out to keep the list to eight; the ideas overlap with substitution and explicitation, and coining new words is taught in Chapter 17.

rows.item: 13. Taboo language: social or religious restrictions on certain practices, expressions, people, places or things
rows.where: Words to remember, Chapter 27; Chapter 27, Step 5
rows.note: Simplified to “words that a society or religion forbids or restricts”, with the Arabic {{اللغة المحظورة}} added.

rows.item: 13. Taboo language is used for realism and emotion, characterisation and humour
rows.note: Shortened to “realism, character or humour”.

rows.item: 13.1 Censorship: institutional censorship and self-censorship
rows.where: Words to remember, Chapter 27; Chapter 27, Step 5
rows.note: Kept as authorities or broadcasters requiring changes versus subtitlers choosing them, with the Arabic {{الرقابة}} added.

rows.item: References (heading only, no entries)
rows.note: The heading was empty; the handbook’s own References list cites the works behind Chapters 26 and 27.

rows.item: A section near the end, on using digital tools and machine translation wisely and effectively, as a practical guide for beginner translators
rows.note: Became Chapter 22, in Part 7 (Tools and resources), and widened to include translation memory and CAT tools.

rows.item: A table of common English phrases, their Arabic meanings and, if possible, their Kuwaiti equivalents
rows.note: No such table was made; common expressions appear as lists with Arabic equivalents in Chapters 9 and 15, without Kuwaiti equivalents.

rows.item: Kuwaiti expressions from her Kuwaiti dictionary, with English equivalents: {{الحجي سهل}}, {{الحجي معاك ضايع}}, {{السالفة أكبر من جدي}}, {{الدموع أربع أربع}}, {{الشمس منين طالعة؟}}, {{العين أوسع من الدار}}
rows.where: Chapter 9, Step 5; Chapter 15, Step 1; Chapter 27, Step 3
rows.note: Six expressions were chosen and cited to the dictionary; {{الحجي معاك ضايع}} is used again in Chapter 27, and a Modern Standard Arabic version was added for {{الحجي سهل}}.

rows.item: Simple guidance on using machine translation tools for phrases, while checking and editing the results
rows.where: Chapter 22, Steps 2 to 6; one-page guide “When in doubt”
rows.note: Covers when a machine can help, its typical mistakes, post-editing, better ways to use it and four safety rules; no particular tool is named.

rows.item: A brief guide to useful digital resources (the website Shaikha mentioned and others) and how translators can benefit from them
rows.where: Chapter 3, Steps 2 and 3; Chapter 21, Step 3; Chapter 22, Step 1
rows.note: No separate guide: digital dictionaries and term databases (UNTERM, Arabterm) are taught in Chapters 3 and 21, and translation memory and CAT tools in Chapter 22.

rows.item: Practical examples showing how context affects the choice of translation
rows.where: Chapter 7, Step 3 and Try it; Chapter 9, Step 2

rows.note: Given as weak-then-better pairs for Arabic and English, plus a machine’s typical mistakes, instead of one separate section.
